title: Amos 5:1–17
context: Amos takes up a funeral lament over Israel as though the nation were already dead: “The virgin of Israel has fallen”. Within the lament, the LORD calls, “Seek me, and you will live”, and warns against the shrines at Bethel, Gilgal, and Beersheba. A doxology to the Maker of the Pleiades and Orion interrupts the charges of injustice in the courts. Quoted speech in this section moves between the LORD’s first person and third-person references to the LORD, and readers need not decide exactly where Amos’s voice and the LORD’s divide. Shared ground: seeking God means seeking good and establishing justice.

verses.text: Listen to this word which I take up for a lamentation over you, O house of Israel:
verses.arminianNotes: Amos announces “a lamentation over you, O house of Israel”. Arminian readers note the force of mourning a nation that still stands: the funeral song is itself a warning, voiced while the hearers can still respond to the call that follows.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the lament as a prophetic declaration that judgment is certain. Shared ground: the prophet grieves rather than gloats, and his sorrow models how God’s messengers announce judgment on God’s people.

verses.text: “The virgin of Israel has fallen; She shall rise no more. She is cast down on her land; there is no one to raise her up.”
verses.arminianNotes: “The virgin of Israel has fallen; She shall rise no more.” Arminian readers read the finality as the sure outcome for the nation as it is, while the calls to seek the LORD that follow still hold out life to those who respond.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the dirge as the certain end of the northern kingdom as a political body, while God preserves a remnant by grace. Shared ground: no one can raise her up except the LORD, and later prophetic hope rests on God alone.

verses.text: For the Lord GOD says: “The city that went out a thousand shall have a hundred left, and that which went out one hundred shall have ten left to the house of Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD says a city that sent out a thousand will have a hundred left. Arminian readers see the shrinking numbers as the cost of persistent rebellion, with a surviving remnant that shows judgment is not total annihilation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same ten percent pattern and see God’s preservation of a remnant as grace within judgment. Shared ground: military loss is the LORD’s doing, and a small remainder survives the disaster.

verses.text: For the LORD says to the house of Israel: “Seek me, and you will live;
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says to the house of Israel: “Seek me, and you will live”. Arminian readers hear a sincere offer of life conditioned on a response that grace enables and people can refuse; the command implies that seeking is truly possible.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear a genuine command and promise, while holding that those who seek do so because God works in them. Shared ground: the offer is real and seeking the LORD is the way of life. The Deuteronomy 10:16 box treats how the command relates to grace.

verses.text: but don’t seek Bethel, nor enter into Gilgal, and don’t pass to Beersheba; for Gilgal shall surely go into captivity, and Bethel shall come to nothing.
verses.arminianNotes: Bethel, Gilgal, and Beersheba were places with sacred histories, yet the LORD forbids seeking them. Arminian readers stress that holy places cannot substitute for the Holy One; going to a shrine is not the same as seeking God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same contrast between religious sites and God himself. The verse includes a wordplay in Hebrew on Gilgal and captivity. Shared ground: Gilgal will go into captivity and Bethel will come to nothing, so trust in places fails.

verses.text: Seek the LORD, and you will live, lest he break out like fire in the house of Joseph, and it devour, and there be no one to quench it in Bethel.
verses.arminianNotes: “Seek the LORD, and you will live” repeats the call, now with the warning that he may “break out like fire in the house of Joseph”. Arminian readers see the urgency of a real choice before the fire comes, with Bethel unable to quench it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the warning as a means God uses to bring his people to himself, alongside the certainty of judgment on the unrepentant. Shared ground: the God they neglect is a consuming fire, and only seeking him gives life.

verses.text: You who turn justice to wormwood, and cast down righteousness to the earth!
verses.arminianNotes: The charge is that they “turn justice to wormwood,” making something sweet and healing into something bitter. Arminian readers see seeking God tied directly to restoring justice; worship cannot be separated from how the courts treat people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the call to seek the LORD cannot be detached from the call to righteousness. Shared ground: perverting justice is a direct offense against God, and the poor suffer when righteousness is cast to the earth.

verses.text: Seek him who made the Pleiades and Orion, and turns the shadow of death into the morning, and makes the day dark with night; who calls for the waters of the sea, and pours them out on the surface of the earth, the LORD is his name,
verses.arminianNotes: The doxology calls Israel to seek the Maker of “the Pleiades and Orion”. Arminian readers see the stars named not for speculation but to show that the God of the heavens is the one Israel has slighted, and he can turn darkness into morning.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see creation and judgment held together: the God who “turns the shadow of death into the morning” also darkens the day. Shared ground: the LORD who orders the stars and pours out the sea is the one Israel must seek.

verses.text: who brings sudden destruction on the strong, so that destruction comes on the fortress.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD “brings sudden destruction on the strong”. Arminian readers note that no fortress protects those who oppose God, and the doxology warns the powerful that their strength is no defense against him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereign power over the mighty, which comforts the oppressed and warns the oppressor. Shared ground: the fortress does not secure those who trample the poor, and God brings sudden destruction on the strong.

verses.text: They hate him who reproves in the gate, and they abhor him who speaks blamelessly.
verses.arminianNotes: “They hate him who reproves in the gate,” the place where legal cases were heard. Arminian readers see a refusal of correction: those who reject honest witnesses close themselves off from the truth that could lead them back to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same hatred of reproof as a sign of hearts set against God’s ways. Shared ground: hostility toward truthful speech in the courts shows a deeper hostility toward the LORD whose justice the gate is meant to reflect.

verses.text: Therefore, because you trample on the poor and take taxes from him of wheat, you have built houses of cut stone, but you will not dwell in them. You have planted pleasant vineyards, but you shall not drink their wine.
verses.arminianNotes: They “trample on the poor” and tax their wheat, and they will not live in their stone houses or drink from their vineyards. Arminian readers see the punishment fitting the crime: wealth gained by oppression will not be enjoyed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the covenant curses of futility at work, where labor yields no lasting good. Shared ground: God reverses the gains of exploitation, and the houses of cut stone and pleasant vineyards will pass to others.

verses.text: For I know how many are your offenses, and how great are your sins— you who afflict the just, who take a bribe, and who turn away the needy in the courts.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “For I know how many are your offenses”. Arminian readers stress that nothing is hidden from him, and the specific sins named are bribery and turning away the needy in the courts, which a people under covenant could have refused.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress God’s complete knowledge of sin and his justice in judging it. Shared ground: injustice against the righteous and the needy is counted by God, and courtroom corruption is a sin he names directly.

verses.text: Therefore a prudent person keeps silent in such a time, for it is an evil time.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore a prudent person keeps silent in such a time, for it is an evil time.” Interpreters debate whether this describes wise caution, sad resignation, or a silence imposed by the coming judgment. Arminian readers often leave it as a lament over corrupt times.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also hold the saying loosely and note that it can describe either the climate of oppression or the dread of judgment. Shared ground: the verse describes an evil time; it does not commend silence in the face of injustice as a general rule.

verses.text: Seek good, and not evil, that you may live; and so the LORD, the God of Armies, will be with you, as you say.
verses.arminianNotes: “Seek good, and not evil, that you may live”. Arminian readers hear the call to seek the LORD in verse 4 restated as a moral call, so that seeking God and seeking good are joined. Israel claimed God was with them, and the condition shows what that claim requires.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the same link between true faith and good works and see the people’s confident claim exposed. Shared ground: the LORD, the God of Armies, is with those who pursue good, not with those who merely say he is.

verses.text: Hate evil, love good, and establish justice in the courts. It may be that the LORD, the God of Armies, will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph.”
verses.arminianNotes: “Hate evil, love good, and establish justice in the courts.” Arminian readers note the humble hope: “It may be that the LORD” will be gracious, which preserves God’s freedom and a real response from the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also stress that grace is never owed; God is free to show mercy to the remnant of Joseph. Shared ground: repentance is shown in public justice, and the outcome rests on God’s grace rather than human leverage.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD, the God of Armies, the Lord, says: “Wailing will be in all the wide ways. They will say in all the streets, ‘Alas! Alas!’ They will call the farmer to mourning, and those who are skillful in lamentation to wailing.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD, the God of Armies, the Lord, announces wailing in every street, with farmers called to mourning. Arminian readers see the lament of 5:1 becoming the experience of the whole land, the fruit of a call refused.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s word of judgment shaping even the cries of the people. Shared ground: the mourning reaches city and countryside alike, and the skilled mourners will have reason to wail.

verses.text: In all vineyards there will be wailing, for I will pass through the middle of you,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will pass through the middle of you,” says the LORD. Arminian readers hear an echo of the Passover night, now turned against Israel, and see the warning that covenant status does not exempt the unfaithful.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also see the exodus imagery reversed and stress that God’s presence brings judgment to the impenitent. Shared ground: the LORD comes near, and for a people who have refused to seek him, his nearness means wailing in the vineyards.
